'''Lucy Florence Oldfield''' (18 September 1925 – 4 July 1989) was a British chemist and Chairman of the London Section of the [[Society of Glass Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theiet.org/publishing/library-archives/the-iet-archives/the-woman-engineer-journal/|title=The Woman Engineer|website=www.theiet.org|access-date=2018-12-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510094311/https://www.theiet.org/publishing/library-archives/the-iet-archives/the-woman-engineer-journal|archive-date=2019-05-10|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was awarded a Glass Slipper for her work in glass technology.

== Early life and education ==
Lucy Florence Oldfield was born on 18 September 1925, to Sidney and Florence Oldfield (née Ambrose) in St Pancras, London.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ancestry.co.uk/account/signin?returnUrl=https%3a%2f%2fwww.ancestry.co.uk%2ffamily-tree%2fperson%2ftree%2f4038397%2fperson%2f6053961851%2fstory|title=Ancestry|website=www.ancestry.co.uk|access-date=2019-07-15}}</ref>

Oldfield was educated at [[Harrow County School for Girls]] and then [[Bedford College, London|Bedford College]], receiving her first Class Honours Degree in Chemistry in 1947.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.sgt.org/lucy-oldfield|title=Lucy Oldfield 1925-1989 – Society of Glass Technology|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-12-13}}</ref> At first Oldfield worked as an analyst for British Drug Houses in London and was eventually accepted as a post graduate research student at [[Imperial College London|Imperial College]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1952 Oldfield was awarded a PhD<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7ibSYLBA6lIC&q=lucy+oldfield+glass+technology&pg=PA330|title=Lucy Oldfield PhD|isbn=9780863411465|last1=Clayton|first1=Sir Robert|last2=Algar|first2=Joan|year=1989}}</ref> for her research in [[electrochemistry]]<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7ibSYLBA6lIC&q=lucy+oldfield+glass+technology&pg=PA330|title=The GEC Research Laboratories, 1919-1984|last1=Clayton|first1=Sir Robert|last2=Algar|first2=Joan|date=1989|publisher=IET|isbn=9780863411465|language=en}}</ref> at Imperial College.<ref name=":0" /> In November 1951, Oldfield had completed her practical work and most of her thesis when she joined the GEC Research Laboratories.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
It was R.W. Douglas<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turner |first=G. L'e |date=November 1974 |title=Technology - A History of Glassmaking. By R. W. Douglas and Susan Frank. Henley-on-Thames: G. T. Foulis, 1972. Pp. xii + 213. £4.50. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-for-the-history-of-science/article/technology-a-history-of-glassmaking-by-r-w-douglas-and-susan-frank-henleyonthames-g-t-foulis-1972-pp-xii-213-450/CDEBCEAD79240D8FB689AC0403F31C26 |journal=The British Journal for the History of Science |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=291–292 |doi=10.1017/S0007087400013510 |issn=0007-0874|url-access=subscription }}</ref> who first engaged Oldfield into the work of glass technology.<ref name=":0" /> Her primary interests were in the structure of glass and the relationship between composition, structure and both physical and electrical properties.<ref name=":0" /> Oldfield's first job in the glass industry was to try and isolate and identify the defects in the TV tube components being manufactured on a Lynch press at the GEC [[Lemington Glass Works]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1975, Oldfield was named as the inventor of a defect-free production process for laser glass.<ref>{{Cite patent|title=Manufacture of laser glass|pubdate=1975-12-30|country=US|number=3929440|assign=[[General Electric Company|General Electric Co. plc]]|inventor1-last=Oldfield|inventor1-first=Lucy Florence}}</ref> Laser glass is used to amplify laser light to the higher energies required for scientific experiments.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Laser Glass|url=https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/how-nif-works/seven-wonders/laser-glass|access-date=2019-05-18|website=lasers.llnl.gov}}</ref>

== Society of Glass Technology ==
In 1958, Oldfield joined the [[Society of Glass Technology]] as a personal member later being awarded with the Fellowship in 1965 and in 1967 she was the second person to receive the London Section Redston Award.<ref name=":0" /> She served on the Board of Fellows in two different positions over three periods.<ref name=":0" /> She was on Council for two periods, 1959 to 1962 and then 1966 to 1969. She was presented as vice president in 1969–1972.<ref name=":0" /> She served the committee for twelve years and was chairman of the London section in 1960–1961.<ref name=":0" /> Oldfield was both a member of the Basic Science and Technology Committee from its inception, and both the Physical Properties Committee and Chemical Analysis Committee.<ref name=":0" /> Additionally, she also represented the Society on [[BSI Group|BSI]] committees dealing with standards for street lanterns and electrical lamps. She also served on the Guilds of London Advisory Committee for the glass manufacturing and process industries.<ref name=":0" />

== Death and commemoration ==
Oldfield died on 4 July 1989 in Harrow, Middlesex, aged 63.

The Society of Glass Technology commemorates Dr Oldfield with the annual Oldfield Award, offering three prizes for research projects carried out by either undergraduate or taught masters students.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oldfield Award |url=https://sgt.org/page/OldfieldAward?&hhsearchterms=%22oldfield+and+award%22 |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=sgt.org}}</ref>
